newsitem.title: USA: Two NY lawmakers agree not to increase pay - group.
newsitem.headline: Two NY lawmakers agree not to increase pay - group.

text.p: Only two incumbent state legislators in New York State have promised not to give themselves a year-end pay increase, according to CHANGE-New York, the state's largest taxpayers' association.

The group said 52 challengers for the state legislature were willing to sign a pledge saying they opposed raising their own pay, but only two incumbents signed on: Assemblyman Jerry Johnson (R-Rochester), and Assemblyman Stephan Kaufman (D-Bronx).

CHANGE-NY cited a similar response to its call for legislators to agree to oppose any attempt to raise taxes. While 49 challengers signed the pact, only five incumbents did so. Including Johnson and Kaufman, they are Richard Anderson (R-Amherst), James Conte, (R-Long Island), and Fred Thiele (R-Sag Harbor).

CHANGE-New York cited speculation the legislature would take up a pay hike when it returns for a special session that Gov. George Pataki has said he plans to call after the November 5 elections to deal with welfare and other issues. It said a rumored pay hike would raise the lawmakers' base pay to $70,000 from $57,500 per year. Most members now also receive guaranteed bonuses ranging from $6,500 to $30,000, CHANGE-New York said.

In mid-October, Pataki said he planned to call a special session after the elections to address welfare. But recently, sources in Albany and New York City have speculated that he may not call a special session, or that any session would address topics other than welfare reform, if the governor determines it might be impossible to reach a quick consensus on that complex and potentially costly issue.
A spokesman for the governor did not immediately return calls for comment about whether a special session is still planned or what it might cover.
There are only a few pressing matters the state legislature must deal with before the end of the year, said a city source, who declined to be identified.

He noted that New York City believes the legislature must meet to extend the city's 12 percent and 14 percent income tax surcharges, which expire on December 31. But he added that there is a school of thought that these surchanges can be retroactively extended after the first of the year.
A spokeswoman for Mayor Rudolph Giuliani had no information immediately available.
